Abstract
Visual object tracking is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Traditional track­
ing methods, which primarily rely on RGB imagery, often face difficulties in complex 
scenarios such as low resolution and background clutter. Hyperspectral imaging, which 
captures both spatial and spectral information across multiple narrow spectral bands, has 
emerged as a promising solution. However, hyperspectral tracking suffers from challenges 
including the complexity of spatial-spectral-temporal modeling, the high dimensionality of 
spectral bands, low spatial resolution, and limited training samples. In response, research­
ers have developed a variety of hyperspectral object tracking (HOT) methods, integrat­
ing innovations in band selection and advanced architectures such as Siamese networks, 
Transformers, and multimodal fusion-based approaches. Despite this progress, existing 
reviews primarily focus on specific sub-domains and provide limited coverage of recent 
developments in hyperspectral video camera technology and the associated data process­
ing pipelines, including calibration and correction techniques. Therefore, this review aims 
to fill that gap by providing an in-depth and systematic overview of HOT. It examines 
the motivations driving this research, highlights recent technological and methodologi­
cal developments, surveys publicly available datasets, and evaluates performance metrics. 
Finally, we discuss future research directions and prospects, offering a valuable resource 
for researchers and practitioners. Moreover, to support ongoing innovation, we have es­
tablished a dedicated GitHub repository to document and continuously update relevant 
works: https://github.com/aamin0102/HOT-Review.

1  Introduction
Visual object tracking (VOT) is a fundamental computer vision task (Yilmaz et al. 2006; 
Yao et al. 2020). Its primary goal is to determine the object’s position and trajectory over 
time, starting from its initial location in the first frame  (Zheng et  al. 2021; Walia and 
Kapoor 2016). VOT has driven numerous applications across diverse domains, includ­
ing video surveillance (Elharrouss et al. 2021), traffic monitoring (Ma et al. 2019), manu­
facturing (Ahmed et al. 2021), healthcare (Kumar and Singh 2024; Ragab et al. 2024), 
autonomous driving (Sharma et al. 2024; Appiah and Mensah 2024), and augmented reality 
(AR) (Li et al. 2024; Baker et al. 2024).
In recent years, the development of tracking algorithms has been dominated by RGB 
and grayscale videos. Traditional methods, such as sparse representation trackers (Zhang 
et al. 2019; Hu et al. 2015), correlation filter-based trackers (Li et al. 2018; Kumar et al. 
2024), and discriminative trackers (Li et al. 2016; Danelljan et al. 2017), primarily rely on 
handcrafted features. While effective in controlled scenarios, these methods often fail in 
complex environments due to limited adaptability to variations in object appearance, light­
ing conditions, and background clutter. The advent of deep learning-based approaches has 
significantly enhanced tracking performance by enabling the automatic extraction of robust 
and discriminative features from large-scale data. Methods leveraging convolutional neural 
networks (CNNs) (Nam and Han 2016), Transformers (Meinhardt et al. 2022), generative 
adversarial networks (GANs) (Song et al. 2018), and reinforcement learning (Yun et al. 
2018) have achieved notable success in handling dynamic and unpredictable environments.
Despite these advancements, RGB-based tracking methods rely on three broad spectral 
bands (red, green, and blue), each integrating a wide portion of the visible spectrum. While 
effective for capturing spatial appearance, this wide-band integration suppresses narrow-
band spectral signatures that are critical for distinguishing materials with similar visual 
textures, particularly under challenging conditions such as low illumination, occlusion, or 
the presence of multiple objects with similar appearances (Islam et al. 2024). Hyperspectral 
imaging (HSI), by contrast, captures data across a dense set of narrow spectral bands span­
ning a wide portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, enabling each pixel to be character­
ized by a detailed spectral signature (Zhao et al. 2025). These spectral signatures enable the 
discrimination of objects and materials based on their inherent properties (Capobianco et al. 
2024), providing valuable cues for applications in remote sensing (Wang et al. 2023; Liu 
et al. 2025), agriculture (Wang et al. 2021), environmental monitoring (Himeur et al. 2022), 
and medical diagnostics (Mangotra et al. 2023). For instance, Fig. 1 demonstrates how the 
HSI color space can distinguish objects that appear visually identical in RGB imagery. In 
such scenarios, players may wear clothing with similar colors and textures, making them 
difficult to differentiate in the RGB color space. In contrast, the HSI representation enables 
clearer discrimination by utilizing differences in spectral characteristics.
Conventional spectral imaging methods, such as spatial or spectral scanning, are too slow 
for real-time applications like object tracking. Recent advancements in low-cost snapshot 
spectral imaging have overcome this limitation, enabling the acquisition of hyperspectral 
videos (HSVs) at video frame rates. This breakthrough has paved the way for tracking mov­
ing objects using spectral, spatial, and joint spatial-spectral information. As a result, HOT is 
emerging as a transformative technology that extends the capabilities of conventional VOT 
and opens new opportunities for precision tracking. This promising field has gained signifi­

Although HOT provides significant advantages, its practical deployment remains chal­
lenging due to several intrinsic properties of hyperspectral video data. In particular, three 
core technical bottlenecks, such as spectral variability, domain shift, and computational 
scalability, fundamentally limit the robustness and generalization of existing HOT systems. 
The key technical challenges can be systematically summarized as follows: 
1.	 Spatial-spectral-temporal modeling: Hyperspectral videos are inherently four-dimen­
sional data (two spatial, one spectral, and one temporal). Most existing tracking archi­
tectures are designed for RGB videos and therefore capture primarily spatial appearance 
cues. Fully exploiting joint spatial-spectral-temporal correlations remains an open 
research problem.

2.	 Spectral variability: The spectral signatures of objects can vary significantly due to 
changes in illumination conditions, atmospheric effects, and material properties. This 
variability makes it difficult to learn stable and robust feature representations for tracking.
3.	 Domain shift: Variations across sensors, spectral ranges, and acquisition conditions 
introduce domain shifts between datasets, which limits the generalization capability of 
existing models. For instance, the HOT2023 and HOT2024 datasets provide data across 
three distinct spectral domains, VIS (16 bands), NIR (25 bands), and RedNIR (15 bands), 
each capturing different portions of the electromagnetic spectrum. A model trained on 
one domain may therefore fail to generalize to another, highlighting the practical signifi­
cance of domain shift in HOT.
4.	 High dimensionality and computational scalability: The large number of spectral 
bands increases discriminative power but also introduces high-dimensional inputs, 
redundant information, and significant computational cost. Efficient processing and band 
selection are therefore critical for real-time applications.
5.	 Low spatial resolution: Hyperspectral sensors inherently involve a trade-off between 
spatial and spectral resolution, resulting in coarse spatial details and mixed pixels contain­
ing multiple materials, which complicates accurate localization and feature extraction.
6.	 Limited training samples: Unlike RGB tracking, where large-scale annotated datasets 
are readily available, hyperspectral video acquisition is costly and time-consuming. This 
scarcity of training samples constrains the development of deep models and limits their 
generalization ability.
Moreover, while RGB-based tracking has been comprehensively reviewed (Xu et al. 2019; 
Chen et al. 2022), HOT remains comparatively underexplored, with only two dedicated sur­
veys available to date. Qian et al. (2024) provided an initial overview of conventional HOT 
methods, datasets, and evaluation protocols, submitted in mid-2023. Wang et al. (2025), 
submitted in late 2024, focused primarily on a subset of deep learning–based approaches.

between accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. By addressing the limitations 
of prior surveys and incorporating recent advances up to mid-2025, this work aims to serve 
as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners. Furthermore, it identifies open 
challenges and outlines promising future research directions to support the development of 
more robust, scalable, and generalizable HOT systems. The main unique contributions of 
this survey are as follows: 
1.	 First end-to-end comprehensive review of HOT: We provide the first survey that sys­

datasets, metrics, and algorithms, offering a complete foundation for the HOT field.
2.	 In-depth analysis of hyperspectral imaging and calibration: Unlike prior reviews, we

3.	 Comprehensive methodological coverage: We summarize recent developments in HOT,

2  Hyperspectral imaging and video sensors
In this section, we provide the foundational background necessary for understanding HOT. 
The discussion is organized into three components: (1) hyperspectral imaging and its appli­
cations; (2) hyperspectral video cameras, with a focus on recent advancements in real-time 
acquisition systems; and (3) data calibration.
2.1  Hyperspectral imaging
HSI is an advanced imaging technique that captures the spectral properties of light across 
numerous narrow wavelength bands, extending beyond the visible spectrum into the infra­
red and ultraviolet regions (Kim et al. 2012). The spectral range of HSI is illustrated in 
Fig. 3. Unlike conventional RGB imaging, which is limited to three broad bands, HSI pro­
vides detailed spectral information at each pixel, thereby significantly enhancing the ability 
to discriminate and analyze materials (Johansen et al. 2020).
The process of HSI involves collecting reflectance data across multiple wavelengths to 
generate a continuous spectral profile for each pixel (Qian 2021). This produces a multidi­
mensional data structure known as a hypercube, where two dimensions encode spatial infor­
mation, and the third encodes spectral information across multiple wavelength bands. An 
example hypercube is shown in Fig. 4, with the spectral signature of a single pixel illustrated 
on the right. These detailed spectral signatures enable precise material characterization and 
identification, supporting a wide range of real-world applications, including:

2.2  Hyperspectral video sensors
Hyperspectral video sensors represent a major advancement in imaging technology, 
enabling continuous capture of both spatial, spectral, and temporal information over time. 
Traditional hyperspectral imaging systems, often limited to static scenes, rely on sequen­
tial scanning techniques such as push-broom (line-scan) (Gamez et al. 2012) and whisk-
broom (point-scan) (Foresti and Busetto 2018), which acquire data line by line or point by 
point, respectively. This sequential acquisition constrains temporal consistency (Wang et al. 
2018), rendering such systems less suitable for dynamic environments and real-time appli­
cations such as object tracking.
To address these limitations, snapshot hyperspectral imaging techniques have emerged as 
a promising solution, enabling the acquisition of complete spatio-spectral cubes in a single 
exposure. Two prominent architectures used for HOT are mosaic snapshot spectral imaging 
and coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI).
2.2.1  Mosaic snapshot spectral imaging
Mosaic snapshot cameras capture both spatial and spectral information in a single exposure 
through the integration of a spectral filter array (SFA) directly onto the image sensor. Each 
filter transmits a specific narrow spectral band, allowing each pixel to record intensity at 
a defined wavelength. The filters are arranged in a repetitive mosaic pattern, producing a 
mosaic spectral image. An example is the XIMEA snapshot VIS camera with 16 spectral 
bands built on an imec sensor, which is shown in Fig. 5, illustrating both the physical cam­
era and the schematic of its SFA-based imaging process (Hou et al. 2022).
Early developments in filter array design include the color filter array (CFA) in RGB 
imaging, with the Bayer pattern (Bayer 1976) as a classic example. The Bayer CFA employs

In CASSI, spatial and spectral information is optically encoded onto a 2D detector via 
coded apertures and dispersive optical elements (Wagadarikar et al. 2008). The coded aper­
ture modulates incoming light using a pseudo-random binary or grayscale mask, while the 
disperser introduces wavelength-dependent spatial shifts (Liang 2020). The detector thus 
records a multiplexed 2D projection of the original 3D cube, which is computationally 
reconstructed using sparsity-based algorithms (Willett et al. 2013; Martín et al. 2014). A 
schematic of the CASSI architecture is shown in Fig. 7.
Several CASSI variants have been developed, distinguished by dispersive arrangements 
and coding strategies to balance resolution, fidelity, and complexity:
	
●
Single Disperser CASSI (SD-CASSI): Employs one dispersive element (Meng et al. 
2020), achieving high spectral resolution but introducing spatial blurring in raw meas­
urements (Wagadarikar et al. 2008).
	
●
Dual Disperser CASSI (DD-CASSI): Uses two opposing dispersers to cancel blur 
while preserving spectral modulation  (Gehm et  al. 2007), producing measurements 
closer to the scene and simplifying reconstruction, though with slightly reduced spectral 
resolution (Zhang et al. 2024).
	
●
Dual-Coded Spectral Imager (DCSI): Replaces static masks with programmable 
modulators (Lin et al. 2014), using a digital micromirror device for spatial coding and a 
liquid crystal on silicon device for spectral coding (Wang et al. 2018). This decoupling 
allows dynamic measurement control and improves reconstruction.
	
●
Spatial-Spectral Coded Spectral Imager (SSCSI): Simplifies hardware by using a 
single coded aperture for spatially varying spectral modulation (Wang et al. 2018). This 
compact design retains joint coding benefits while reducing system complexity, achiev­
ing high reconstruction fidelity under sparsity constraints (Gündüz et al. 2024).
Beyond these optical configurations, recent hybrid approaches integrate CASSI with emerg­
ing sensing paradigms. For example, Geng et al. (2024) integrate CASSI with event-based 
neuromorphic sensing. Their system combines asynchronous event streams, which capture 
brightness changes with microsecond latency, with spatial-spectral CASSI measurements 
fused by a deep neural network. This approach enables ultra-high-speed hyperspectral video 
with millisecond temporal resolution, outperforming conventional frame-based systems in 
dynamic scenes.

2.2.3  Other approaches
Bian et al. (2024) introduced nanostructure-based sensors fabricated via photolithography 
that capture high-dimensional spectral, spatial, and temporal information. Their system 
achieves 124 FPS with inline-eq-IEq1 4

2.3  Data processing and calibration
Raw data acquired by spectral video cameras requires careful calibration to correct dis­
tortions and ensure consistency across spectral bands. In mosaic snapshot systems, each 
pixel records light from a distinct wavelength determined by the underlying SFA, which 
introduces spectral and spatial non-uniformities. Additional factors such as sensor imperfec­
tions, optical aberrations, and non-uniform illumination further contribute to fluctuations in 
intensity and spectral response (Khonina et al. 2025). Calibration involves five stages: (1) 
dark calibration; (2) white calibration; (3) spectral calibration; (4) image registration; and 
(5) color conversion.
2.3.1  Dark calibration
Dark calibration removes fixed-pattern noise produced by the sensor in the absence of light. 
This noise, often caused by thermal effects or sensor electronics, can significantly degrade 
spectral accuracy. Following imec’s guidelines, Xiong et al. (2020) acquired a dark frame inline-eq-IEq17 
by covering the camera lens with an opaque cap, ensuring that no light reached the sensor.

2.3.4  Image registration
Image registration geometrically aligns two or more images so that corresponding pixels refer 
to the same scene point. This step is crucial in multimodal datasets, such as HOT2020 (Xiong 
et al. 2020), where both RGB and hyperspectral images are provided. Multimodal registra­
tion often involves images with differing resolutions, spectral characteristics, or fields of 
view. Common strategies include feature-based methods, which match distinctive points 
(e.g., corners, edges) across modalities, and intensity-based methods (Myronenko and Song 
2010), which optimize similarity metrics across entire regions. Once correspondences are 
established, a transformation (e.g., affine or projective) is applied. Accurate registration 
enables effective cross-modal fusion for applications such as object detection and tracking, 
material classification, and scene understanding (Zhang et al. 2021).

2.3.6  Propagation of calibration errors to tracking architectures
Calibration is typically treated as a preprocessing step; however, errors at any stage propa­
gate through the hyperspectral cube and degrade downstream tracking performance. Imper­
fect dark calibration introduces residual additive bias and increased noise variance, thereby 
reducing the effective signal-to-noise ratio across spectral bands (Rogaß et al. 2011), while 
white calibration errors induce multiplicative distortions in reflectance. These perturbations 
alter pixel-wise spectral distributions and weaken inter-object separability.
The impact of such distortions depends on the tracking architecture and its underly­
ing modeling assumptions. Correlation Filter (CF)-based trackers, which rely on regression 
in the Fourier domain and assume relatively stable appearance statistics (Liu et al. 2021), 
are particularly sensitive to additive and multiplicative perturbations that degrade response 
peak sharpness and increase drift during online updates. In contrast, Transformer-based 
trackers embed spectral-spatial patches into token representations and model dependencies 
through self-attention (Wang et al. 2023). Although global attention can mitigate localized 
noise, systematic spectral bias introduces distribution shifts relative to the training data, 
affecting embedding consistency, normalization behavior, and attention weighting.
Moreover, spectral miscalibration caused by inaccurate correction matrices perturbs 
narrow-band reflectance signatures (Liao et al. 2025), weakening material-level discrim­
inability. Registration errors further disrupt spatial correspondence, degrading correlation 
estimation in CF methods and positional consistency in Transformer architectures. Since 
tracking operates sequentially, calibration artifacts accumulate through template or memory 
updates, amplifying long-term drift. These observations highlight that calibration quality 
directly affects feature stability and ultimately determines the robustness of hyperspectral 
tracking systems.

3.1  Datasets
We briefly describe the widely used datasets in HOT research, highlighting their character­
istics, modalities, and associated challenges.
3.1.1  DIRSIG dataset
Uzkent et al. (2018) released a synthetic aerial hyperspectral dataset generated using the 
DIRSIG software. The dataset covers a spectral range of 400–1000 nm at 10 nm intervals. 
It comprises 157 frames, with an average ground sampling distance of 0.3 m and a frame 
rate of 1.42 FPS. Due to its synthetic nature, this dataset is not widely used for evaluation.
3.1.2  HOT challenge dataset
Xiong et al. (2020) released the first large-scale hyperspectral video tracking dataset, con­
sisting of 50 videos in the visible range (470–620 nm). To ensure data quality, dark calibra­
tion and spectral correction were performed: the former eliminated sensor noise, while the 
latter reduced second-order responses using the manufacturer-provided correction matrix. 
RGB sequences were also collected for the same scenes; however, they were not accurately 
aligned in space and time, limiting their value for cross-modal evaluation. To compensate, 
the dataset included false-color sequences derived from hyperspectral data. A further limi­
tation is its relatively narrow spectral range, which reduces representativeness for broader 
HOT applications. Originally, only testing sequences were included, but the dataset was 
later extended to 75 videos (40 training, 35 testing), which served as the benchmark for the 
first HOT challenge in 2020.
In 2022, the HOT committee released an additional 45 hyperspectral videos (HOT2022 
dataset), comprising 28, 000 frames with a maximum of 1000 frames per sequence and an 
average of 625 frames per sequence. Compared with earlier datasets, HOT2022 increased 
attribute diversity by introducing camera motion (Table 1). Nevertheless, it remained lim­
ited to the visible spectrum, restricting evaluation under conditions where near-infrared or 
broader bands could provide advantages.
In 2023, the HOT committee expanded the datasets from HOT2020 and HOT2022, 
resulting in 302 videos and more than 100, 000 frames. The dataset includes 110 training, 
87 validation, and 105 ranking sequences. A major advancement was the inclusion of near-
infrared (25 bands, 665–960 nm) and red-near-infrared videos (15 bands, 600–850 nm), 
enabling broader spectral analysis. However, only hyperspectral and false-color sequences 
are available, with no aligned RGB data, which limits multimodal benchmarking. Another 
important feature of HOT2023 is its strong spectral variability across sequences, which 
enhances realism but presents challenges for tracker generalization. This variability makes 
it a valuable benchmark for developing robust HOT models.
The HOT2024 dataset was further expanded to 409 videos, with 217 training, 117 vali­
dation, and 75 ranking sequences. HOT2024 introduces unprecedented scale and diversity, 
with substantial spectral variability across sequences that create domain shifts and make 
tracker generalization more demanding. This variability enhances realism and establishes 
HOT2024 as a challenging benchmark that encourages the development of robust models 
capable of adapting to diverse spectral conditions.

While success and precision plots emphasize accuracy, FPS measures computational effi­

4.1  Spectral band selection and regrouping for HOT
Spectral band selection and regrouping are pivotal components in HOT, addressing the high 
dimensionality and redundancy inherent in hyperspectral video. Unlike RGB video, which 
contains only three broad channels, hyperspectral video consists of dozens or even hundreds 
of narrow bands. While this richness provides unique spectral signatures that differentiate 
materials, it also imposes significant computational overhead. Moreover, the same target 
may appear differently across bands, making it desirable to select optimal bands for specific 
scenarios.
Band selection and regrouping methods can be broadly categorized into traditional hand­
crafted approaches and deep learning-based approaches. Importantly, both paradigms per­
form spectral band selection or transformation, mapping the hyperspectral cube into one or 
multiple pseudocolor representations. The key distinction lies in how band importance is 
determined, either through predefined statistical or heuristic criteria, or through deep learn­
ing mechanisms such as attention or feature adaptation. In several deep learning frame­
works, hard or near-binary attention weights are employed to select informative bands and 
group them into pseudocolor representations.

4.1.3  Computational cost vs performance trade-off in band selection methods

computational efficiency and tracking performance. Traditional band selection methods 
generally offer lower computational complexity and faster inference, making them suit­

designed criteria may limit their ability to capture complex spectral-spatial dependencies

4.2  Conventional HOT
Before the advent of deep learning, HOT predominantly relied on conventional pipelines 
built on handcrafted features and correlation-filter-based tracking frameworks. These 
methods were explicitly designed to exploit the rich spectral information of hyperspec­
tral imagery through manually engineered descriptors and similarity measures. While such 
approaches were computationally efficient and interpretable, they fundamentally lacked 
data-driven representation learning, which limited their ability to jointly model spatial-spec­
tral-temporal (SST) dependencies. As a result, conventional HOT methods often struggled 
under spectral variability, illumination changes, target deformation, and background clut­
ter–conditions that are prevalent in modern benchmarks such as HOT2023 and HOT2024.
Conventional HOT pipelines consist of two stages: feature extraction and tracking frame­
works. Although these components were progressively refined, they were generally opti­
mized independently, preventing holistic modeling of appearance evolution across space, 
spectrum, and time.
4.2.1  Feature extraction
Feature extraction plays a central role in conventional HOT, as hyperspectral videos provide 
dense spectral signatures alongside spatial structure and temporal continuity. Early methods 
primarily focused on spectral information, leveraging the fact that hyperspectral reflectance 
curves encode material-specific characteristics that can facilitate object discrimination. 
For instance, Banerjee et al. (2009) employed reflectance-based features for illumination-
invariant tracking, while Uzkent et al. (2016) improved robustness by constructing local 
hyperspectral histograms that adapt to lighting variations.
Despite their effectiveness in controlled settings, purely spectral descriptors exhibit 
inherent limitations. Hyperspectral measurements are often affected by spectral mixing

dimensions independently or combine them through shallow feature concatenation. This 
design limits their capacity to capture higher-order nonlinear dependencies between bands 
and spatial context, making them sensitive to spectral variability, occlusion, and background 
interference–issues that become particularly pronounced in cluttered or highly dynamic 
environments.
Several works attempted to explicitly model spectral variability over time. MHT (Xiong 
et al. 2020) assumes fixed spectral signatures across frames, which limits adaptability under 
illumination or pose changes. DMT (Xiong et al. 2019) relaxes this assumption by model­

However, such temporal modeling remains local and largely linear, which restricts robust­

encode spatial and spectral information, though their rigid structure limits adaptation to 
significant shape deformation or appearance change. Chen et al. (2022) further improved 
robustness by extracting spatial-spectral features directly from mosaic hyperspectral images, 
thereby avoiding distortions introduced by spectral rearrangement or demosaicking.
More recently, some conventional pipelines have adopted transfer-learning-inspired 
strategies by compressing hyperspectral data into three-channel or single-band representa­

et al. 2016). While this approach enables the reuse of powerful convolutional filters, it inevi­
tably discards inter-band continuity and material-specific spectral information. As a result, 
feature extractors optimized for RGB statistics struggle to preserve the physical meaning 
of hyperspectral signatures, reducing their ability to distinguish objects with similar spatial 
textures but distinct spectral characteristics.

The introduction of correlation-filter-based approaches marked an important step toward

into training to reduce boundary artifacts and improve target-background discrimination. 
Similarly, TASSCF (Tang et al. 2022) integrated HOG and CN features into the LADCF 
framework (Xu et al. 2019), which jointly optimized spatial feature selection and temporal 
consistency, resulting in more stable tracking across longer sequences.
Despite these improvements, correlation-filter-based frameworks remain fundamentally 
limited in hyperspectral tracking. Small spatial misalignment, illumination-induced spectral 
shifts, or nonlinear appearance changes can cause substantial variation in high-dimensional 
spectral responses, leading to filter drift and degraded discrimination. These limitations 
become particularly evident on challenging benchmarks such as HOT2023 and HOT2024, 
where increased spectral variability and background clutter reduce the reliability of hand­
crafted spectral descriptors and linear correlation-filter models.
In summary, conventional HOT frameworks laid essential groundwork by integrating 
spectral similarity measures, handcrafted descriptors, and efficient correlation filters. Their 
key strengths include computational efficiency, interpretability, and modest robustness 
improvements through background-aware and temporally constrained learning. However, 
their reliance on fixed spectral assumptions, rigid feature designs, and shallow fusion strate­
gies severely limits their ability to model complex SST dependencies. As demonstrated in 
Sect. 5, these limitations result in consistently inferior performance compared to modern 
deep learning approaches, which can dynamically learn nonlinear spatial-spectral-temporal 
representations and better handle real-world tracking challenges.

more robust and adaptive tracking solutions. Consequently, numerous trackers have been

remains consistent over time. In hyperspectral imagery, however, the spectral signature 
of an object may vary substantially even when its spatial appearance remains unchanged. 
Such variations can alter the underlying feature representation and undermine similarity-
based matching. This limitation is further amplified when RGB-pretrained backbones are 
employed, as these models primarily encode spatial texture and shape rather than wave­
length-dependent material properties. Addressing this limitation may require spectrum-
aware metric learning, adaptive band-selection strategies, or domain-adaptive similarity 
modeling capable of explicitly accounting for spectral distribution shifts.
4.3.2  Transformer-based HOT
Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm in visual tracking by leveraging self-
attention mechanisms to model long-range dependencies and global contextual relation­
ships (Chen et al. 2021, 2023; Xie et al. 2022). Unlike correlation-based Siamese trackers 
that rely primarily on local similarity matching, Transformers enable global feature interac­
tion between template and search regions. The pioneering TransT (Chen et al. 2021) intro­
duced ego-context augment (ECA) and cross-feature augment (CFA) modules (Fig. 12) to 
fuse template and search features through attention mechanisms, significantly improving 
localization accuracy over traditional correlation-based frameworks. Motivated by these 
advances in RGB tracking, Transformer architectures have recently been extended to hyper­
spectral object tracking, where modeling complex spectral-spatial dependencies is essential 
due to the high dimensionality and strong inter-band correlations of hyperspectral imagery.

improved target discrimination. MSFFT (Islam et al. 2023) adopts a three-branch Siamese

problem largely unresolved.

enabling global reasoning over spectral-spatial features and improving tracking perfor­

constrained by three fundamental challenges: the reliance on RGB-pretrained backbones 
that do not fully capture hyperspectral reflectance properties, the use of fixed spectral rep­

explicit mechanisms for spectral alignment between template and search regions. Address­
ing these limitations will likely require spectrum-aware pretraining strategies, adaptive 
spectral alignment mechanisms, and attention architectures specifically designed to exploit 
the unique spectral structure of hyperspectral data.

multiple spectral bands into three channels, discarding subtle material signatures that dis­

degraded tracking performance.
Subsequent work refined fusion mechanisms to balance modality contributions more

including HOT2023 and HOT2024. These datasets introduce greater spectral diversity and 
cross-scene variation, where the spectral distributions of targets and backgrounds vary sig­
nificantly across environments. Under such conditions, improved fusion alone cannot com­
pensate for unresolved spectral misalignment between modalities. This observation further 
indicates that spectral domain shifts, rather than insufficient fusion capacity, remain a pri­
mary factor limiting cross-dataset generalization in hyperspectral object tracking.

hyperspectral embeddings into large RGB foundation models. In this paradigm, hyperspec­

4.3.4  Transfer learning-based HOT
Transfer learning has played a central role in advancing HOT by reusing RGB-pretrained fea­
ture extractors to mitigate the scarcity of annotated hyperspectral data. Early studies showed 
that pretrained CNNs can be adapted to hyperspectral tracking through fine-tuning and 
architectural modifications. For example, TLHT (Yiming et al. 2021) integrates a VGG-M 
backbone with hyperspectral-specific layers and combines it with the MDNet (Nam and Han 
2016) tracking framework. This approach demonstrates that spatial features learned from 
large RGB datasets can provide useful initialization for hyperspectral tracking, particularly 
when targets are distinguishable by structural appearance. Several studies also incorporate 
adversarial learning through the VITAL framework (Song et al. 2018) combined with band-
selection strategies. Trackers such as BABS (Islam et al. 2023), BAE-Net (Li et al. 2020), 
and SST-Net (Li et al. 2021) extend VITAL (Song et al. 2018) with hyperspectral-specific 
components to suppress background interference and enhance target-distractor separation.
However, RGB-pretrained networks encode strong inductive biases toward texture, 
edges, and spatial semantics, while lacking explicit wavelength awareness. Consequently, 
they capture appearance patterns rather than material reflectance characteristics, which are 
often the key discriminative cues in hyperspectral imagery. This mismatch limits the effec­
tiveness of transfer learning when targets and backgrounds exhibit similar spatial structures 
but differ primarily in spectral signatures. As spectral diversity and inter-band variability 
increase, fine-tuning alone becomes insufficient to bridge the representational gap between 
RGB and hyperspectral domains (Fig. 13).
Detection-based transfer learning has also been explored in HOT. Hy-Tracker (Islam 
et al. 2024) adapts the YOLO (Redmon et al. 2016) detection framework to hyperspectral

a practical means to improve efficiency while maintaining competitive tracking accuracy.

Dynamic template update mechanisms are widely employed to adapt trackers to 
gradual changes in appearance. For instance, HA-Net (Liu et al. 2021) selects the most

et al. 2022), and Deep-SCT (Zhao et al. 2023) employ similar update strategies. These 
approaches perform well when target appearance evolves smoothly, and confidence scores 
reliably reflect tracking quality. However, they implicitly assume temporal continuity and 
stable spectral responses. Under conditions such as illumination changes, partial occlusion, 
or abrupt motion, confidence estimates may become unreliable, resulting in incorrect tem­
plate updates and gradual model drift.
Attention-based temporal modeling attempts to address this issue by selectively 
weighting informative frames. HSPTrack  (Wang et  al. 2023) integrates temporal atten­
tion to modulate frame contributions, while SPIRIT (Chen et al. 2023) performs template 
updates only when confidence thresholds are satisfied. These mechanisms help suppress 
noisy frames and improve robustness under moderate occlusion. Nevertheless, attention 
weights are derived from learned feature similarities that remain sensitive to spectral shifts. 
When spectral distributions change significantly across scenes, attention mechanisms may 
incorrectly emphasize misleading frames, leading to unstable tracking.
Recurrent architectures provide an explicit mechanism for modeling temporal depen­
dencies across frames. Hy-Tracker (Islam et al. 2024), for example, incorporates GRU mod­
ules to refine predictions and enforce temporal coherence. Recurrent models are effective 
when motion patterns are smooth and predictable, as hidden states can capture consistent 
temporal dynamics. However, their performance may degrade in scenarios involving abrupt 
motion or strong spectral variation, where the assumptions of motion continuity and sta­
ble feature representations become less reliable. In such cases, propagated hidden states 
may accumulate errors over time, leading to degraded tracking accuracy. This limitation 
is reflected in the reduced performance of Hy-Tracker (Islam et al. 2024) on HOT2024 
compared to HOT2020 (Tables 9 and 7), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining reliable 
recurrent states under rapidly changing spectral-temporal conditions.

enhance memory perception, while token fusion and temporal decoders (Chen et al. 2025b)

improve robustness under prolonged occlusion and complex motion patterns. However, the 
increased architectural complexity and reliance on extended temporal memory substantially 
raise computational demands and data efficiency requirements, limiting scalability and 
practical deployment, particularly in resource-constrained or real-time HOT applications.

5  Experimental results and discussion
We evaluated a diverse set of HOT methods across five widely used datasets. Since bench­
marking standards and available implementations vary, tracker results were aggregated 
from published manuscripts wherever possible, and otherwise reproduced from released 
frame-by-frame results using the standardized evaluation metrics defined in Sect. 3.2.
5.1  Trackers, data collection, and evaluation protocol
Different datasets are associated with different subsets of trackers, reflecting the variety 
of benchmarking standards and the availability of implementations in the field. To ensure 
transparency and reproducibility, we describe below the evaluation protocol, result sourcing 
strategy, and potential sources of inconsistency across the aggregated comparisons.
5.1.1  Evaluation protocol
All trackers are evaluated under a one-pass evaluation (OPE) setting, in which each tracker 
is initialized from the ground-truth bounding box in the first frame and runs without re-ini­
tialization for the remainder of the sequence. Performance is quantified using two standard 
metrics: Distance Precision (DP@20pixels), defined as the percentage of frames in which 
the predicted center location falls within 20 pixels of the ground-truth center, and Success 
Rate (AUC), computed as the area under the success plot of bounding-box overlap ratios 
across a range of IoU thresholds. These metrics align with established RGB tracking bench­
marks such as OTB (Wu et al. 2013) and GOT-10k (Huang et al. 2019), enabling partial 
cross-paradigm comparison where applicable.

5.2  Quantitative analysis
To systematically evaluate the performance of recent HOT approaches, we analyze results 
across five benchmark datasets: HOT2020, HOT2023, HOT2024, IMEC25, and WHU-Hi-
H3. Each method is assessed using two standard metrics: AUC and DP@20pixels, which 
jointly measure overall accuracy and spatial localization precision. We also consider run­
time efficiency (in FPS) and methodological design, providing insight into the trade-offs 
between accuracy, complexity, and adaptability. Below, we present detailed findings for 
each dataset.
5.2.1  HOT2020 dataset
The HOT2020 dataset provides a balanced benchmark with diverse scenes, motions, and 
spectral characteristics. Table 7 presents the quantitative results on this dataset, from which 
several key observations can be drawn: (1) fusion-based methods achieve the highest over­
all accuracy, with TFTN (Zhao et al. 2022a) attaining the best AUC of 0.764 and preci­
sion of 0.962; (2) Transformer-based methods offer a strong accuracy–speed balance, with 
SSTtrack (Chen et al. 2025) achieving AUC of 0.713; (3) Siamese-based methods provide 
competitive accuracy at higher inference speeds, making them suitable for real-time appli­
cations; (4) knowledge distillation methods such as SiamOHOT (Sun et al. 2023) and Sia­
mPKHT (Qian et al. 2023) achieve the highest FPS values of 38 and 43, respectively, with 
moderate accuracy; and (5) traditional CF-based methods remain the most computationally 
lightweight but achieve comparatively lower accuracy due to their reliance on handcrafted 
features.
TFTN (Zhao et al. 2022a) employs parallel HSI and RGB feature extractors followed by 
a Transformer-based fusion module, enabling complementary exploitation of fine-grained 
hyperspectral cues and structural RGB context. This design mitigates spectral redundancy 
while improving robustness in cluttered backgrounds. SSTtrack (Chen et al. 2025) intro­
duces a spectral–spatial adapter and a temporal condition adapter, which together enhance 
spectral discrimination and stabilize predictions under fast motion or appearance changes. 
These components explain its strong performance on HOT2020, where spectral variability 
and temporal complexity often degrade simpler architectures.
Among Siamese-based trackers, BRRF-Net  (Ouyang et  al. 2021) and HA-Net  (Liu 
et  al. 2021) achieve competitive accuracy while maintaining relatively high efficiency.

5.2.4  IMEC25 dataset
The IMEC25 dataset contains only near-infrared domain sequences, unlike HOT2023 and 
HOT2024, which include videos captured across diverse spectral domains. This reduced 
spectral diversity lowers the need for domain adaptation mechanisms and partly explains 
why both classical CF-based methods and modern deep trackers achieve competitive per­

observations can be drawn: (1) Transformer-based methods deliver the strongest overall

variability; and (5) the domain adaptation module of DaSSP-Net (Li et al. 2025) has limited 
impact on this dataset compared to spectrally diverse benchmarks, suggesting that adapta­

The WHU-Hi-H3 dataset is particularly challenging for hyperspectral object tracking, fea­
turing camouflaged targets, low target–background contrast, and strong spectral similar­

this dataset, from which several key observations can be drawn: (1) fusion-based methods 
achieve the highest overall accuracy, with SiamCAT (Jiang et al. 2024) attaining the best

the best CF-based AUC of 0.568, but struggle significantly under camouflage-rich condi­

between fusion-based and CF-based methods is notably larger on this dataset than on other

highly similar spectral signatures.

differences in the statistical properties of the underlying feature distributions, particularly 
those associated with background clutter and target-background separability.

5.7  Discussion and future research directions
Drawing on the methodological review and experimental analysis presented in this sur­
vey, several critical research directions emerge for advancing hyperspectral object track­
ing. While prior work has identified high-level challenges, many of these directions remain 
insufficiently grounded in concrete algorithmic formulations. In the following, we outline 
key research problems and discuss technically actionable strategies to address the systemic 
limitations identified in Sects. 4-5, including limited cross-dataset generalization, scarcity 
of hyperspectral training data, and the lack of spectral-aware evaluation protocols.
1. Unified band selection strategy
Current HOT benchmarks exhibit significant spectral variability across datasets, 
with models optimized for one spectral configuration often failing to transfer to others. 
UBSTrack (Islam et al. 2025) partially mitigates this issue by generating fixed three-band 
false-color representations, regardless of the number of bands in the HSI; however, such 
projections inherently discard high-dimensional spectral dependencies and limit discrimina­
tive capacity. Therefore, future research should pursue:

2. Domain adaptation for cross-dataset generalization
Even with unified band selection, significant covariate shift persists due to differences in 
sensor characteristics, illumination conditions, and scene composition. Existing approaches 
such as DaSSP-Net (Li et al. 2025) partially address this issue but still exhibit substantial 
performance degradation across diverse HOT datasets. Future research directions include: 
(i)

(ii)	 Spectral normalization, leveraging adaptive instance normalization with domain-
specific parameters to mitigate the influence of source-domain statistics and improve 
robustness during target-domain inference;
(iii)	 Spectral contrastive adaptation, constructing positive pairs from same-material regions 
across different sensors and negative pairs from distinct materials, thereby encouraging 
domain-invariant spectral representations while suppressing sensor-specific artifacts;
(iv)	 Test-time adaptation, where entropy minimization or self-supervised objectives are 
used to adapt lightweight model components during inference on unlabeled target data, 
which is particularly relevant for satellite and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) plat­
forms with continuously changing spectral environments.

clutter, and complex motion. RGB-based transfer learning cannot substitute for spectral 
supervision. Future dataset construction should address: 
(i)	
Acquisition pipeline design, involving synchronized capture using hyperspectral sen­

4. Generative modeling and foundation models
Data scarcity and the reliance on RGB-based pretraining remain major bottlenecks in

(i)	 Hyperspectral foundation models, analogous to DINOv2  (Oquab et  al. 2023) or

through CLIP-style contrastive pretraining  (Radford et  al. 2021) on paired spectral

with spectral characteristics for more flexible and interpretable tracking.

Spectral evaluation metrics, such as the Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), to explicitly 
measure spectral consistency between predicted and ground-truth target signatures. 
Representative approaches include spectral angle-based similarity measures, spectral 
reconstruction error, and composite spatial-spectral metrics that jointly account for 
localization accuracy and spectral agreement;
(ii)	 Composite training objectives that jointly optimize spatial localization and spectral 
fidelity by combining conventional spatial losses with spectral consistency terms, with

6. Multi-object hyperspectral tracking
Existing HOT benchmarks focus primarily on single-object tracking, whereas real-world 
applications in surveillance, remote sensing, and precision agriculture often involve multi­
ple interacting targets with overlapping spectral signatures and complex occlusion patterns. 
Multi-object hyperspectral object tracking (MOHOT) introduces challenges beyond those 
encountered in RGB-based multi-object tracking, including: 
(i)	
Spectral identity maintenance under occlusion, where overlapping objects produce 
mixed spectra that require spectral unmixing (e.g., Fully Constrained Least Squares or 
deep unfolding architectures) to disentangle individual target signatures;
(ii)	 Graph-based spectral association, in which graph neural network (GNN)-based track­
let association modules encode pairwise spectral similarity and spatial proximity as 
edge features, enabling joint spectral-spatial reasoning, followed by assignment via the 
Hungarian algorithm;
(iii)	 Cross-target spectral attention, where transformer-based architectures model inter­
actions between targets to suppress shared spectral background components while 
enhancing discriminative inter-target spectral differences;
(iv)	 Benchmark design, emphasizing datasets with spectrally similar targets, dense occlu­
sion events, and diverse spectral ranges, along with evaluation metrics such as multi-
object tracking accuracy (MOTA), multi-object tracking precision (MOTP), and 
spectral re-identification accuracy.
7. Reproducibility and standardization
A significant proportion of existing HOT methods lack publicly available implementa­
tions, hindering reproducibility and fair comparison. This fragmentation slows methodolog­

establish: 
(i)	
Open-source code and model release, including training pipelines, pretrained weights, 
and evaluation scripts, to ensure reproducibility and enable fair comparison across 
methods;
(ii)	 Reference preprocessing APIs with documented calibration parameters and paired raw/
calibrated data releases, enabling controlled ablation of preprocessing effects;
(iii)	 Unified benchmark platforms analogous to GOT-10k (Huang et al. 2019), enforcing 
one-pass evaluation with no test-time tuning and integrating spectral metadata (sensor 
model, spectral range, calibration coefficients) into submissions;

8. Multi-modal data fusion
Multi-modal fusion of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) with complementary modalities such 
as RGB, LiDAR, or radar provides a principled solution to the limited spatial resolution of 
HSI and its sensitivity to adverse sensing conditions. The central challenge lies in learning 
robust cross-modal representations under heterogeneous spatial resolutions, noise charac­
teristics, and sensing geometries. Key research directions include: 
(i)	
Pansharpening and dynamic registration, where low-resolution hyperspectral cubes 
are fused with high-resolution RGB imagery via deep pansharpening networks (He 
et al. 2019), combined with online motion compensation using optical-flow-based or 
feature-based registration to correct temporal misalignment caused by platform motion;
(ii)	 Uncertainty-aware cross-modal attention, in which modality-specific confidence 
scores derived from model calibration or uncertainty estimation are incorporated into 
attention mechanisms to adaptively weight HSI and RGB contributions, enabling fall­
back to RGB when the hyperspectral signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is degraded;
(iii)	 Learnable wavelet front-ends, which decompose hyperspectral signals into localized 
spectral-frequency components prior to nonlinear representation learning, thereby pre­
serving multiscale structure and improving feature robustness. This is motivated by 
recent findings that rational dilated wavelet transforms enhance representation stability 
in complex spectral domains (Siino et al. 2025);
(iv)	 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)–hyperspectral fusion for all-weather HOT, where het­
erogeneous SAR backscatter and HSI reflectance feature spaces are aligned via con­
trastive representation learning on paired acquisitions of the same scene.
9. Balancing accuracy and efficiency
Real-time HOT on resource-constrained platforms, such as UAVs and embedded sensing 
systems, requires domain-specific model compression strategies that explicitly exploit the 
unique properties of hyperspectral data. Key technically grounded directions include: 
(i)	
Hyperspectral-aware structured pruning, which leverages high inter-band correlation 
to identify redundant spectral filters using gradient-based saliency or activation-based 
importance metrics, enabling aggressive compression (e.g., inline-eq-IEq19575% parameter reduc­

(ii)	 Spectral knowledge distillation, where a full-band teacher network transfers spectral-
spatial representations to a reduced-band or lightweight student model, facilitating 
deployment on hardware with fixed or limited spectral sensing capabilities; and
(iii)	 Hyperspectral-specific neural architecture search (NAS), exploring search spaces that 
incorporate spectral-spatial separable convolutions, wavelength-aware operators, and 
dilated depthwise spectral convolutions, subject to explicit latency and memory con­
straints for embedded deployment.

6  Conclusion
This paper presents a comprehensive overview of hyperspectral object tracking, bringing 
together the full pipeline from data formation to methodological design and empirical evalu­
ation. Beginning with hyperspectral imaging and video sensors in Sect. 2, we described 
how sensor architectures, acquisition mechanisms, and calibration procedures shape the 
spectral-spatial characteristics of hyperspectral video data. This hardware- and data-focused 
foundation is essential for understanding the constraints and opportunities that distinguish 
HOT from traditional RGB tracking.
We then reviewed commonly used datasets and evaluation metrics in Sect. 3, which estab­
lish the experimental conditions under which HOT methods are trained and assessed. These 
datasets highlight the scarcity and diversity challenges inherent in hyperspectral video, 
while the evaluation protocols clarify the performance criteria used across the community.
Building on this context, in Sect. 4, we categorized existing HOT algorithms into spectral 
band selection and regrouping strategies, conventional approaches, and deep learning-based 
frameworks. This structure reveals how different classes of methods attempt to exploit spec­
tral information, manage high dimensionality, and integrate spatial-spectral cues for robust 
tracking. The experimental comparisons in Sect.  5 further connected these algorithmic 
choices to practical performance, illustrating how design decisions translate into accuracy, 
efficiency, and generalization behavior.
Despite rapid progress, HOT still faces several fundamental challenges, as discussed 
throughout this survey. First, the high computational cost of processing high-dimensional 
spectral data limits real-time deployment (Sect. 5.5). Second, the scarcity of large-scale 
annotated hyperspectral video datasets (Sect. 3) restricts the development and generaliza­
tion of data-driven models. Third, achieving strong cross-dataset generalization remains dif­
ficult due to variations in spectral distributions, sensor characteristics, and scene conditions 
(Sect. 5.6). These challenges motivate the future research directions outlined in Sect. 5.7.
By linking these research directions directly to the limitations identified in earlier sec­
tions, this survey provides a clearer and more actionable roadmap for advancing HOT. We 
hope that synthesizing insights across hardware, calibration pipelines, datasets, and algo­
rithms will support continued progress toward robust and efficient hyperspectral object 
tracking in real-world applications.
